newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan factions start U.N.-sponsored peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Afghan factions start U.N.-sponsored peace talks.

text.p: Feuding Afghan factions met in Islamabad under United Nations auspices on Monday in what a U.N. official described as a wide-ranging dialogue for peace.
U.N. special envoy for Afghanistan Norbert Holl told a news conference that the talks, expected to continue on Tuesday and possibly Wednesday, had no formal agenda.
"This was the first meeting that we had today that did not end in disaster," the German diplomat said after the working group of rival factions met for several hours.
"There was a free flow of ideas," he said. "There was a spirit of brotherhood in the meeting."
Holl gave no details and did not say if the two sides had reached agreement on a ceasefire or other peace proposals.

The Islamic Taleban militia was represented by Wakil Ahmad, a Kandahar-based adviser to Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar, along with the Afghan ambassador in Islamabad, Maasoum Afghani, and another diplomat.

They met three nominees of an opposition alliance that has been battling the Taleban north of Kabul and in remote northwestern provinces of Afghanistan since the Islamic militia captured the capital on September 27.

Holl identified them as General Paynda (one name), representing northern General Abdul Rashid Dostum, Mohammad Ishaq, an aide to ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, and Mohammad Rasul Talib, from a Shi'ite Moslem faction.
The United Nations has been trying to persuade the rival groups to agree to a ceasefire, an exchange of prisoners and the formation of a technical committee to oversee the truce.
Success could lead to a dialogue on other issues such as the formation of a broad-based government, demilitarisation of Kabul and creation of a neutral security force for the city.

The Taleban have said in the past that they are ready for a ceasefire and prisoner exchange, but they reject the idea of demilitarising Kabul. They also insist that any future government must rule in accordance with Islamic Sharia law.
The opposition has previously demanded an agreement on the demilitarisation of Kabul as a condition for a ceasefire.
The Taleban, seeking to spread their purist vision of Islam across Afghanistan, now hold more than two-thirds of the country after seizing Kabul and deposing president Burhanuddin Rabbani.
